title: Tinder, kindling and fuel: what each is and how much to gather
asks: what is tinder kindling and fuel
what can i use for tinder
how much kindling do i need
what size sticks to start a fire
what wood burns best for a campfire
my fire keeps going out what am i doing wrong
whats good tindr in the woods
fire wont catch, what goes on first, over
answer: A fire is built in 3 phases, each with larger material: tinder, then kindling, then fuel. If a phase is skipped, the fire is likely to fail.

First set a base and a brace. The base is a flat piece of material, usually wood or a nonporous rock, that keeps tinder and kindling off the wet ground. The brace is a branch about the size of your forearm laid across the base; it helps control the oxygen reaching the fire.
Tinder is a dry material that a small spark, coal or flame can ignite. It is normally fine fibers or petroleum-based.

Natural tinder: birch bark; shredded inner bark from cedar, chestnut and red elm trees; fine wood scrapings or shavings; dead dry grass, ferns, moss, lichen and fungi; dry powdered sap (pitch) from the pine family; crushed fibers from a dead plant; seed down (milkweed, cattail, thistle); feather sticks (wood shavings cut into a piece of wood and still connected to it).
Manmade tinder: cotton balls (most effective coated with a petroleum-based paste), lint, paper, steel wool, a candle, solid fuel tabs.
For a single fire, collect at least enough fibrous tinder to fill a cap or your cupped hand. Petroleum-based tinder is used in smaller quantities because it burns much longer.
Damp natural tinder can be dried before use by storing it between layers of your clothing.
Lay the tinder on the dry base in a mound against the brace. Light it from its bottom edge, on the side away from the brace.

Add kindling when the tinder is burning strong and mostly engulfed by flame. Lay it by the handful across the top of the brace and over the tinder, leaving spaces for the flame to burn through. Laid like a blanket, it cuts off the oxygen and the fire dies out. Lay the next handful perpendicular or diagonal to the first.

Prepare kindling in several sizes, from pencil lead, to pencil, to thumb size, and lay it on in that order. Pieces about 12 to 18 inches long are the easiest to handle. Collect at least a bundle the diameter of a soda can of each size.

Kindling examples: dead, dry small twigs and plant stalks; dead, dry thinly shaved pieces of wood; small dead branches low to the ground on the underside of conifers; larger pieces of wood split down to kindling size.
Fuel: wood at least the diameter of your forearm. Unlike tinder and kindling, fuel does not have to be completely dry if the fire is established well enough to dry it before it burns.

Good fuel is dry, standing dead wood and dry dead branches that snap when broken. Standing or leaning dead wood is usually dry even in rainy climates. Rotten wood lying on the ground is of little use: it smolders and is very difficult to ignite.
Dry, split hardwoods (oak, hickory, ash) give more heat and less smoke than softwoods (pine, spruce, fir). Softwood burns faster and is easy to split.
Split wood to expose the inner wood: it burns faster and hotter than pieces still covered by bark.
warnings: Before building the fire, clear the ground of fallen leaves, vegetation and duff, exposing soil at least 3 feet (1 meter) across, to prevent the fire from spreading along the ground.
Porous rocks contain water and can explode when heated. Do not use them as a base, and remove them from the fire site.
Fuel wood must be free of poison ivy and poison oak. Burned and inhaled, they can cause respiratory distress.
Always split bamboo before burning it: sections can explode.

quotes.text: Fire building occurs across 3 phases. If one phase is skipped even in ideal circumstances, it is likely that the fire will fail due to not having the appropriate mix of oxygen, heat, and fuel. The 3 phases are tinder, kindling, and fuel, each representing an increase in fuel size appropriate for heat and oxygen available to support it.

The base is a flat piece of material, usually wood or a nonporous rock (porous rocks contain water and, when heated, can explode). The base is used to keep moisture susceptible tinder and kindling off the wet ground and provides a clear area to skillfully ignite tinder. The brace is employed across the base to help control oxygen into either the tinder, kindling, or fuel being worked. It is about the size of a person’s forearm. A broken branch can typically be found and employed as a brace.
Porous rock is removed from the fire site, which is at risk of exploding from the heat of the fire.

Tinder is used during the first phase of fire building. A dry material can be ignited by a small spark, coal, or flame. Tinder is normally comprised of fine fibers or is petroleum-based and is either natural or manmade.

Natural tinder examples include— Birch bark—shredded inner bark known as heartwood from cedar, chestnut, red elm trees. Fine wood scrapings or shavings (heartwood preferred). Dead dry grass, ferns, moss, lichen, and fungi. Dry powdered sap from the pine tree family also known as pitch. Fine pitch wood scrapings or shavings. Crushed fibers from a dead plant. Pine pitch globules mixed with fibrous material. Seed down (milkweed, cattail, thistle). Feather sticks (wood shavings cut into and still connected to a piece of wood).

Manmade tinder examples include— Cotton balls (most effective when coated with a petroleum-based paste). Lint. Paper. Foam rubber. Hexamine. Tryoxine. Commercial petroleum-based pastes. Steel wool. Gunpowder. Candle. Solid-state fuel tabs.

When using fibrous tinder to start a single fire, isolated persons collect enough to fill their patrol cap or their hand with fingers cupped at a minimum. A sufficient amount of tinder must be used to generate a hot enough flame to ignite kindling in the next phase of fire building. Smaller quantities of petroleum-based products are used as they burn much longer with a central burn point.
Isolated persons can procure natural tinder, when damp, and store it between layers of clothing to use heat radiated by the body to dry it prior to use.

Tinder is laid on a dry base to avoid the fine fibers from soaking up moisture and rendering it unusable. When laid on the base it rests up against the brace in a mound. The tinder is lighted from its bottom edge away from the brace.

Kindling is added once the tinder is burning strong and mostly engulfed by flame. It is laid by the handful on, and perpendicular to, the top of the brace and over the burning tinder. It should be laid over the tinder fire so that some spaces are left in the kindling for the tinder fire to burn through. If the kindling is laid over the tinder like a blanket, the fire will likely not receive enough oxygen to continue burning, will not be able to ignite the kindling, and will die out. The second handful of kindling is laid perpendicular or diagonal to the first laid kindling to maintain small pockets for the fire to burn through and grow.

Preparing kindling in several different sizes that range from pencil lead, to pencil, and then to thumb size will make fire-building easy when laid over the tinder in that order. Kindling that is approximately 12 to 18 inches in length is the easiest to apply and manipulate when building a fire. Isolated persons collect at the very minimum; the diameter of a soda can of each size, to ensure enough kindling is available to increase the fire’s heat to ignite the fuel in the next phase.
Dead, dry, small twigs and plant stalks; isolated persons should consider that during the winter months live deciduous vegetation that is dormant may appear dead.
Dead, dry, thinly shaved pieces of wood, bamboo, or cane (always split bamboo as sections can explode).

Small branches low to the ground on the underside of coniferous trees that are dead from lack of sun (a single branch often has all three sizes of kindling on it that simply need to be broken down for use).
Larger pieces of wood split into kindling-sized pieces.
Clear the ground of fallen leaves, vegetation, and duff; expose 3 feet (1 meter) in diameter of soil at a minimum to prevent the fire from spreading along the ground.

Wood used as fuel should be the diameter of the forearm at a minimum. Wood is the most abundant source of fuel in most environments; however, there are many other types of fuel an isolated person can use.
Unlike tinder and kindling, fire fuel does not have to be kept completely dry if the fire is established well enough to dry the damp fuel before burning.

Effective fuel sources include dry, standing, dead wood and dry, dead branches (those that snap when broken). Standing or leaning dead wood is usually dry even in rainy climates as its vertical position sheds most rain. In contrast, rotten wood, most of which is found lying directly on the ground, is of little use since it smolders and is very difficult to ignite.
Dry, split hardwood trees (such as oak, hickory, and ash) are less likely to produce excessive smoke and provide more heat than softwoods (pine, spruce, and fir) due to their higher density.
Softwood burns faster and produces more smoke unless a large flame is maintained. They are often straight grained, have fewer knots, and are easy to split.

The inner wood of dead branches and small diameter trees is the driest because it is not exposed to the weather. Wood that is split to expose the inner wood grains burns faster and hotter than wood pieces that are covered by bark which naturally protects trees from fire and collects moisture.
Wood used as fuel must be free of poisonous plants such as poison ivy or poison oak. These plants can cause respiratory distress if burned and inhaled.

Checked against ATP 3-50.21 ch. 5: three phases, base and brace (forearm-size brace; porous rock explodes), tinder definition and natural/manmade lists (the card rightly drops the manual's mislabel of inner bark as 'heartwood' and omits gunpowder/hexamine), cap-or-cupped-hand quantity, petroleum tinder in smaller amounts, drying tinder in clothing, mound against the brace lit from the bottom edge away from the brace, kindling by the handful with gaps (blanket smothers it), next handful perpendicular/diagonal, pencil-lead to thumb sizes, 12-18 in, a soda-can bundle of each, fuel at least forearm diameter, damp fuel acceptable once established, standing dead wood, rotten wood smolders, hardwood vs softwood, split wood burns hotter; warnings (3 ft cleared soil, porous rock, poison ivy/oak smoke, split bamboo). Order of the build is correct. Minor (recommended, not blocking): the kindling-examples line drops the source's caveat that in winter dormant live deciduous vegetation may appear dead, which is exactly the 'my fire keeps going out' failure; add it back. Kind fact acceptable: it mixes definitions with the build order.
